intro: It's a rough week for OpenAI's safety narrative — a former insider just called the company's safety culture "broken" in *The Atlantic*, and CEO Sam Altman isn't exactly helping by telling the world to accept "bad things" like hacks and scams as the price of AI progress. Meanwhile, the tension between AI enthusiasm and AI anxiety is playing out everywhere: Google had to freeze its bug bounty program because AI-generated slop overwhelmed it, the White House is trying to rebrand the whole field as "super intelligence," and a billion people are using ChatGPT every month even as public opinion sours — proving that our complicated relationship with this technology is only getting more complicated.

stories.title: Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman
stories.summary: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, stated in an interview that the world should accept 'bad things' happening with AI, such as hacks and scams, in exchange for the benefits the technology provides. He called for a lighter regulatory approach, citing the 'good stuff' AI can deliver. His comments drew immediate backlash from critics of major AI companies, and came after one of OpenAI's safety experts resigned.
stories.opinion: Altman's framing presents a false dichotomy — that society must simply accept harms like hacks and scams as an inevitable cost of AI progress, rather than actively working to mitigate them through thoughtful regulation and safety measures. Responsible development doesn't require choosing between innovation and safety; it requires pursuing both. The timing, following a safety researcher's resignation, raises legitimate questions about whether this framing serves to deflect from internal safety c…

stories.title: How OpenAI uses ChatGPT Sites (live at DevDay!) | Kath Korevec (Product Lead)
stories.summary: Kath Korevec, a Product staff member at OpenAI working on Codex, demos ChatGPT Sites live at OpenAI DevDay 2026. She spent over a year building and using Sites internally before public launch, and has shipped Plugin Insights, MCP plugin hosting, and the connector ecosystem (~60 integrations). The episode covers how to turn Slack, Notion, and calendar data into internal tools that adapt to each team member. Key topics include: Plugin Insights and how it changes site accessibility, an incident command site built with live Slack/Notion connectors, using Codex to wire up connectors, the infrastructure layer inside Sites, creative uses like fixing a Spotify playlist using Reddit and computer use, a community dungeon crawler game showcasing collaborative skill distribution, bringing inference into Sites via widgets, and Kath's prompting strategy. She draws a hard line on AI acting in her name…
stories.opinion: This is a solid product demo episode that showcases ChatGPT Sites as OpenAI's play for internal tooling and low-code app building — essentially competing with Retool, Glide, and similar platforms but with AI-native connectors and natural language configuration. The most interesting signals are: (1) the connector ecosystem hitting 60 integrations suggests OpenAI is serious about enterprise workflow integration, (2) Plugin Insights appears to be an analytics/observability layer that could differe…

stories.title: People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?
stories.summary: The article by Will Douglas Heaven in MIT Technology Review explores the paradox that while public sentiment toward AI is increasingly negative — with majorities expressing nervousness, opposing data centers, and ranking AI less popular than ICE — usage continues to skyrocket, with ChatGPT hitting a billion monthly users and half of US adults using chatbots. The author argues these aren't two separate groups but largely the same people, and that the hatred is directed not at the technology itself but at the relentless corporate push to embed AI everywhere and the looming social and economic upheaval it threatens. He draws parallels to social media's similar love/hate dynamic, but notes that with AI there may still be a chance to shape the outcome differently.
stories.opinion: The article captures a genuine and important tension in public attitudes toward AI. The framing is compelling — that people hate the hype machine and corporate coercion more than the underlying technology — and rings true. The social media parallel is apt but slightly underexplored; the piece was cut off before fully developing the argument about what makes AI different. The observation that optimism correlates with lower adoption (Global South vs. Global North) is provocative and deserves deep…

stories.title: Can Safeworld convince people that GenAI robots won’t hurt them?
stories.summary: Safeworld, founded by CMU Safe AI lab director Dr. Ding Zhao along with Kyle Wong and Simo Rachidi, has emerged from stealth with over $12 million in seed funding led by Shine Capital and a16z Speedrun. The company builds simulation environments populated with realistic digital human models to safety-test GenAI-powered robots before real-world deployment. Their platform creates digital replicas of specific environments (like factory floors), inserts the robot's actual control software, and runs thousands of scenarios to identify dangerous edge cases — such as blind corners, human falls, or unexpected behaviors. The founders argue that as robots move into unstructured environments at scale, third-party safety validation will be essential, both for technical assurance and for building public trust.
stories.opinion: Safeworld is tackling a genuinely important and timely problem. As humanoid robots powered by generative AI models move from demos to real-world deployment, the gap between 'works in a controlled setting' and 'safe around unpredictable humans at scale' is enormous. The third-party validation angle is smart — robot makers have an inherent conflict of interest in self-certifying safety, and regulators will eventually demand independent testing, much as they do for vehicles and medical devices. Th…

stories.title: An OpenAI safety insider calls the culture 'broken'
stories.summary: David Robinson, who spent 3.5 years at OpenAI leading safety reports for 12 frontier launches and drafting the company's Preparedness Framework, resigned and published an essay in The Atlantic calling OpenAI's safety culture 'broken.' He argued that the relentless pace left his team too busy sprinting to consider or implement meaningful changes, and that AI labs should operate with the redundancy and rigor of nuclear plants and airports. His departure follows OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing sensitive information with an outside safety group, and echoes earlier warnings from former superalignment co-lead Jan Leike that safety had taken a backseat to product development.
stories.opinion: Robinson's critique carries significant weight because he wasn't an outside critic or a brief visitor — he was the person literally writing OpenAI's safety rulebook for three and a half years. When the author of your safety framework says the culture makes it impossible to actually follow through on safety, that's not a philosophical disagreement, it's an operational indictment. The nuclear plant analogy is apt: those industries learned through catastrophic failures that speed and safety are fu…

stories.title: OpenAI is sticking more ads in ChatGPT
stories.summary: OpenAI is expanding advertising in ChatGPT by introducing visual ads featuring images of sponsored products and services. Testing begins in the US later this month, initially appearing alongside AI-generated images. This builds on text-based ads introduced in February 2025. The visual ads will remain separate from generated content and won't appear for Plus, Pro, or Enterprise subscribers. OpenAI says it has guardrails to avoid showing ads in sensitive contexts.
stories.opinion: This is a predictable but notable step in OpenAI's monetization strategy. Placing image ads alongside AI-generated images is a natural advertising surface, but it raises questions about the long-term user experience of free-tier ChatGPT. The 'initially' qualifier in their announcement strongly signals ads will expand to other parts of the product over time. It's a classic freemium squeeze: degrade the free experience enough to push conversions to paid tiers while also capturing ad revenue from…

stories.title: ﻿The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for? | Michael Jacobs
stories.summary: The article discusses UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's upcoming G20 presidency in 2027, arguing it presents a significant opportunity to advance a progressive agenda on the global stage. Despite Burnham's stated preference for focusing on domestic policy, columnist Michael Jacobs contends that chairing the G20 will require him to address urgent international issues including AI regulation and climate action, and that this platform could be used to tackle challenges at the intersection of technology, food systems, and the global economy.
stories.opinion: The article makes a reasonable case that G20 presidencies are underutilized opportunities for host nations to shape global discourse, and that the UK under Burnham should not treat it as merely ceremonial. However, the piece reflects a common tendency in political commentary to overestimate the transformative potential of multilateral summits, which historically produce more communiqués than concrete action. The tension Jacobs identifies between Burnham's domestic focus and global responsibilit…

stories.title: Google froze its open source bug bounty program due to a ‘significant rise’ in AI submissions
stories.summary: Google has paused its Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program (bug bounty) as of October 1, 2026, due to being overwhelmed by AI-generated submissions. The company cited a 'significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid,' with engineers and open source maintainers struggling under reports that were invalid or contained hallucinations. Google plans to provide an update in Q1 2027 and has directed participants to its other bug bounty programs in the meantime. This follows warnings from cybersecurity experts last year that AI slop posed a serious risk to bug bounty programs.
stories.opinion: This is a predictable consequence of making powerful text generation tools widely available without adequate safeguards against misuse. Bug bounty programs rely on a high signal-to-noise ratio — expert researchers submitting genuine, validated vulnerabilities. When the cost of generating a plausible-sounding but hallucinated vulnerability report drops to near zero, the economics break down entirely. The real damage here is twofold: legitimate security researchers lose a revenue stream and incen…

stories.title: Our minds aren’t equipped to handle AI
stories.summary: The article argues that the longstanding metaphor of the brain as a computer is fundamentally limited and that AI products, built on this flawed assumption, are cognitively harmful. Drawing on neuroscience and evolutionary history, author Benjamin Riley contends that human cognition is far more complex than the input-computation-output model suggests, citing figures like John von Neumann who doubted computational models could capture the nervous system's complexity. Riley compares AI to junk food for the mind — immediately appealing but ultimately undermining cognitive systems developed over millennia. The piece challenges the reductive views of tech leaders like Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk who equate brains to biological computers, suggesting this oversimplification is causing real damage as AI products push deeper into culture.
stories.opinion: The article raises a genuinely important point that gets lost in most AI discourse: the computational metaphor for the mind is just that — a metaphor, and an incomplete one. The comparison to junk food is evocative and apt in some ways; there is real concern that offloading cognitive labor to AI could atrophy skills the way processed food undermined nutrition. However, the article appears to commit a version of the naturalistic fallacy — assuming that because our cognitive systems evolved over…

stories.title: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czar
stories.summary: President Donald Trump has appointed Jay Clayton, the current Director of National Intelligence, to serve concurrently as the new White House AI czar. Clayton, who oversees 18 US intelligence agencies, has a background as a former top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and former SEC chairman during Trump's first term. During his confirmation hearing, Clayton described AI as both a 'gamechanger' and 'a threat.'
stories.opinion: Appointing the intelligence chief to simultaneously serve as AI czar is a notable consolidation of power that signals the administration views AI primarily through a national security lens rather than as a broader economic or social policy issue. While Clayton's experience with financial regulation at the SEC could bring useful oversight instincts, the dual-hatting raises questions about whether one person can adequately manage both the sprawling intelligence community and the complex, fast-mov…

stories.title: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem?
stories.summary: The Trump administration has officially rebranded 'artificial intelligence' as 'super intelligence' via executive order, and hosted major tech CEOs — including leaders from Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, and others — to sign a 'Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.' The pact is described as 'deeply non-binding' legally, with Trump calling it 'morally binding' instead. TechCrunch's Equity podcast hosts were skeptical the commitment would have real impact, with Kirsten Korosec suggesting the meeting was primarily a rebranding effort to separate the positive narrative of 'super intelligence' from public fears about AI taking jobs or being dangerous. The episode also noted the rapid shift in tone, as just weeks earlier Trump had dismissed any need for AI safety measures, and Anthropic had been out of favor with the administration before CEO Dario Amodei attended a private dinner that app…
stories.opinion: This is largely political theater dressed up as policy. Renaming AI to 'super intelligence' does nothing to address legitimate concerns about job displacement, safety risks, or concentrated corporate power — it just swaps the label. A non-binding pact signed by CEOs who have every financial incentive to avoid real regulation is essentially meaningless from an accountability standpoint. The speed at which the administration went from dismissing safety concerns to hosting a safety summit suggests…

stories.title: NJ’s former Lt Gov is using AI to say he’s innocent of sexual harassment
stories.summary: New Jersey's former Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell, who resigned on September 25th after an investigation found he had sexually harassed a staffer and violated ethics rules, attempted to use AI chatbots to defend himself during a media interview on NJ PBS. Caldwell claimed he ran the investigation report through multiple AI platforms 59 times and that none of them found grounds for a sexual harassment finding. The article notes that AI chatbots are notoriously sycophantic, tending to tell users what they want to hear, making this an unreliable method of exoneration.
stories.opinion: This story highlights a troubling but predictable misuse of AI: treating chatbot responses as authoritative validation. Caldwell's approach is fundamentally flawed because AI language models are not legal analysts or fact-finders — they generate responses based on patterns and are well-documented to exhibit sycophantic behavior, essentially agreeing with the framing of whatever question is posed to them. The way you prompt an AI dramatically shapes its output, so asking it 'what would your find…
